request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital Course: The patient, a 92-year-old Caucasian female with a medical history significant for Alzheimer's dementia, seizure disorder, osteoporosis, and osteoarthritis, was admitted for evaluation of new onset confusion and constipation. Review of symptoms revealed anorexia, weight loss, constipation for the last three weeks, and history of a fall one month prior to the presentation. An MRI of the brain showed lytic lesions and serum protein electrophoresis and urine protein electrophoresis confirmed the diagnosis of Multiple Myeloma. Primary Hyperparathyroidism was also suspected due to high intact PTH levels. Hypercalcemia was managed during the admission, and the patient was started on medication. The patient was later discharged and is currently following up with oncology services as an outpatient on a low dose of lenalidomide with a stable M protein. 

Disposition: Discharged

Major Procedures: N/A

Brief hospitalization course: A 92-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the hospital due to confusion and constipation. During the admission, the patient was diagnosed with Multiple Myeloma and Primary Hyperparathyroidism. Hypercalcemia was managed, and the patient was later discharged and is currently following up with oncology services as an outpatient.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The condition established after investigation as chiefly responsible for the admission is multiple myeloma. The patient presented with confusion and constipation, and both are best explained by hypercalcemia. The hypercalcemia in turn was attributed to myeloma, with lytic lesions on MRI and confirmatory protein electrophoresis, though primary hyperparathyroidism was also suspected on the basis of a high PTH.

Two candidates compete for principal diagnosis. Hypercalcemia (E83.5) is a manifestation, and myeloma is the underlying cause that was diagnosed and worked up. Primary hyperparathyroidism (E21.0) was only suspected. In ICD-10-AM, myeloma is coded to C90.0 (multiple myeloma). The hypercalcemia was managed during the stay, but the final diagnosis centres on the malignancy, so I chose C90.

CODE: C90
